name: British Heart Foundation: information, support, CPR and defibrillators (charityevals, 2025-26)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: health information, the Heart Helpline, peer support, CPR training and the defibrillator network in the UK.
summary: The British Heart Foundation's health and support work in the UK, year to March 2026. About three quarters of this spending is information and support: health information pages (35 million views, most of them from the UK), the Heart Matters magazine and printed guides, the nurse-led Heart Helpline (26,000 people) and online peer support, modelled from trials of patient education for coronary heart disease (a fifth fewer deaths and better quality of life, at a small fraction of a trial programme's dose for one call or a few pages read). The rest is CPR training through the free RevivR app (190,000 people trained) and The Circuit, the national defibrillator network, modelled from cardiac-arrest survival registries. The result, about 0.005 years of healthy life per $1,000, is far below the site's global-health median because a page read or a call is a tiny dose of education, much of it would reach patients from the NHS anyway, cardiac arrests are rare and three in four already get bystander CPR; every branch is discounted for missing data, since BHF measures no outcomes. The dose of education a reader or caller gets is the biggest uncertainty, and the result is mostly uncertainty (the range spans orders of magnitude).

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: BHF's spending on information, support, CPR and defibrillators in the year to 31 March 2026: its health expenditure less the judged shares for policy and implementation pilots (modelled in the main model), with fundraising and the shops' net loss spread over all charitable spending. From the audited accounts.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: People who completed RevivR CPR training in the year (the Circuit branch reaches every cardiac arrest in the UK, in the effect section); the Heart Helpline's and the peer community's users; readers of the web pages and printed information who live with cardiovascular disease.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: RevivR: the chance a trainee is at a cardiac arrest in the years their training lasts, times how much more often trained bystanders do CPR, times the survival gain from bystander CPR. The Circuit: arrests where a bystander uses a defibrillator found through the network, times the survival gain from a bystander's shock. Information and support: the people reached, in trial programmes' worth of patient education (each channel's dose), times the trials' fall in deaths and gain in quality of life.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Each branch has its own trust in its evidence (registries for CPR and defibrillators, education trials for information), counterfactual, share of credit and missing-data step (Convention 4); the canonical rows are deaths-weighted averages, for reading only.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for illness counted in DALYs in a units-of-value model (docs/normalization.md 2.6): the healthy years are put into units of value by the shared conversion, which the headline's conversion cancels, so they move only with their own sliders. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: Deaths averted, valued at the site's value of a death by age, plus the information branch's quality-of-life gain through the bridge, in units of value per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Health expenditure (information, support, CPR, policy), year to 31 March 2026 (£)

source.title: British Heart Foundation, Annual Report and Accounts 2025-26, group statement of financial activities

rows.explainer: BHF's second charitable activity: awareness, the Heart Matters magazine, the nurse-led Heart Helpline, health information, CPR (RevivR) and the defibrillator network (The Circuit), healthcare implementation grants (£7.8m of health awards, note 11), and policy (p. 67, p. 28-36). The accounts give no split by activity.

rows.label: Share of health expenditure on CPR training and defibrillators
rows.explainer: RevivR (an app and schools programme, built with Laerdal), The Circuit (a national database and its support for 80,000 defibrillator guardians), community defibrillator and CPR grants and campaigns. The £4.6m Omaze house draw raised for The Circuit is a sense of scale for a year's spending on it (p. 33). Our judgment: about £8m of the £54m, the rest being information, the magazine and helpline, awareness campaigns, implementation grants and policy.

rows.label: Share of health expenditure that is policy and influencing work (modelled in the research-and-policy model)
rows.explainer: The same judgment as in british-heart-foundation-charityevals, where the policy work is modelled (the smokefree-generation law): policy and public affairs teams in four nations, campaigns and the £1.0m grant to Action on Smoking and Health (note 11). Here it only takes that spending out of this model's cost. Change it in all three places together (both models and the charity record's weights).

rows.label: Share of health spending on Healthcare Implementation Fund pilots
rows.explainer: The fund pays NHS teams to test new ways of delivering care (cholesterol injections in pharmacies, home blood-pressure checks after pregnancy, health checks for taxi drivers, lung screening; p. 22, 29). The accounts give £7.9m of health grants: £1.0m to ASH and £6.9m of other health grants not itemised (note 11), up from £3.0m of health awards the year before (note 4). The fund has awarded £5.74m in all (BHF's fund page, retrieved 2026-11-04), its earliest listed round in March 2024, so roughly £2–3m a year; the rest of the other health grants is most likely community CPR and defibrillator grants (in cpr_share_of_health) and nurse and professional awards. Our judgment: 5% of health spending (£2.7m with its staff), 3% to 13% (the high end if most of the other health grants were pilots). It is modelled in british-heart-foundation-charityevals with the research it resembles; keep the two models and the charity record's weights in step.

rows.label: Share of health spending on information, the Heart Helpline, Heart Matters, peer support and awareness
rows.explainer: Everything else in health spending: the health information pages (35 million views), the Heart Matters magazine, the nurse-led Heart Helpline, online peer support, accessible and printed information, and awareness campaigns (p. 29-31). About 74% at the judged shares. Awareness campaigns have no chain of their own: campaigns on heart-attack symptoms shorten the delay to hospital in about half the studies and not in the rest (Hoschar et al., Open Heart 2020, 18 interventions), and BHF's paid 'Keep us beating' campaign also raises its profile with donors; their benefit is in other_unmodelled_share.

rows.label: Cost of information, support, CPR and defibrillator work, including overhead
People who completed RevivR CPR training in the year

source.title: British Heart Foundation, Annual Report and Accounts 2025-26, trustees' report
source.quote: In the last year alone, more than 190,000 people across the UK completed training

rows.explainer: RevivR teaches in about 15 minutes how to recognise a cardiac arrest, do CPR and use a defibrillator; 500,000 people have completed it so far, and nearly 1,700 schools use the classroom version. BHF's own count of completions (an app records them); it isn't independently verified, which is in implementation_adj.

rows.label: Cost per person trained (all three branches' cost over RevivR's trainees, for reading only)
Years a trainee stays readier to do CPR
rows.explainer: CPR skill decays within months of training, but knowing to call, push hard and fast and fetch a defibrillator, and being willing to, last longer; the Resuscitation Council recommends refreshing every year or two. Our judgment: 3 years on average, 1 to 6.

rows.label: Heart Helpline: people who contacted the nurses in the year

source.title: British Heart Foundation, Annual Report and Accounts 2025-26
source.quote: 26,000+ people contacted our Heart Helpline in 2025–26, with a 93% satisfaction rate

rows.explainer: Specialist cardiac nurses answer questions from patients and families by phone and email: one conversation each, usually about a diagnosis, a medicine or living with a condition. BHF's own count.

rows.label: Online peer support: people using the community each month

source.title: British Heart Foundation, Annual Report and Accounts 2025-26
source.quote: More than 8,800 new members joined last year, with around 9,000 people actively using the community each month

rows.explainer: BHF's moderated community on HealthUnlocked, including a new heart-failure group (over 1,000 members). The monthly count stands for the year's users: more people visit once, fewer keep coming, which the dose below takes in.

rows.label: Health information web pages: views in the year

source.title: British Heart Foundation, Annual Report and Accounts 2025-26
source.quote: 35m+ views to our health information web pages

rows.explainer: Page views, not people: one reader opens several pages (the next row).

rows.label: Share of the web pages' views from the UK
rows.explainer: The 35 million views are worldwide. Similarweb puts 62% of bhf.org.uk's desktop traffic in the UK (retrieved 2026-11-04), with the United States and India next; mobile readers of health pages skew more to the UK. Our judgment: 65% from the UK, 55% to 85%. Only UK readers are counted, so the beneficiaries stay the UK.

rows.label: Web pages viewed per reader in the year
rows.explainer: No visitor count is published. Similarweb's estimate for bhf.org.uk is 2.26 pages per visit (retrieved 2026-11-04), and some readers come back during the year: about 1.3 visits each gives 3 pages per reader, 1.5 to 8.

rows.label: Readers of BHF's printed and accessible information, including Heart Matters
rows.explainer: BHF distributed over 150,000 Easy Read, large-print and braille copies, and audio, sign-language and translated materials were used 118,000 times (p. 31); the free quarterly Heart Matters magazine and the printed booklets hospitals hand out publish no circulation. Our judgment: 300,000 people a year, from the 150,000 accessible copies (the low end) to 600,000 with the magazine and booklets.

rows.label: Share of readers who live with heart or circulatory disease
rows.explainer: More than eight million people in the UK live with cardiovascular disease (p. 30), and the pages are about conditions, tests and medicines, so many readers are patients; others are their families and carers, students, health workers and people checking a symptom. Patients only, since the effect is from trials in patients (carers' help to the patient is in other_unmodelled_share): our judgment 22%, 10% to 40%.

rows.label: People with cardiovascular disease in the UK reading BHF's information in the year
Out-of-hospital cardiac arrests with resuscitation attempted, per person per year (England, 2024)

source.title: Resuscitation Council UK, 2025 Resuscitation Guidelines: Epidemiology of cardiac arrest

rows.explainer: 54 per 100,000 a year in England (the Resuscitation Council's annual incidence, from the Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Outcomes registry, which records arrests where an ambulance crew attempts resuscitation, the ones bystander CPR can change). Across the UK's 69 million that is about 37,000, below the 43,000 attempts the same page gives for the UK, since the other nations' rates are higher; England's rate is kept as the trainees' chance, a little low.

rows.label: People present at an arrest who could start CPR
rows.explainer: Most arrests happen at home with one or two family members present; public arrests have more bystanders. With the incidence this is a trainee's chance of being at an arrest, assuming trainees are as likely as anyone to be there (they skew younger and to workplaces and schools, while arrests skew to older people at home, so the low end is 1).

rows.label: Yearly chance a trainee is at a cardiac arrest where resuscitation is attempted
rows.explainer: In this model the baseline is the arrest itself: without CPR almost every one is fatal (the survival gain below is the change).

rows.label: How much more likely a trained bystander is to give CPR (percentage points)
rows.explainer: In England bystanders already give CPR in 72.6% of attempted resuscitations (Resuscitation Council UK, 2024 data), much of it coached by the 999 call handler, so training can add at most the remaining quarter, plus better compressions and fetching a defibrillator. Studies of prior training find trained bystanders start CPR more often; our judgment: 15 points, 5 to 30.

rows.label: Survival gain from bystander CPR before the ambulance arrives (percentage points)

source.title: Hasselqvist-Ax et al. (2015), NEJM 372:2307 (abstract, Europe PMC)
source.quote: The 30-day survival rate was 10.5% when CPR was performed before EMS arrival versus 4.0%

rows.explainer: Adjusted for the arrest's circumstances the odds ratio is 2.15 (95% CI 1.88 to 2.45), which on the 4.0% baseline is 8.2% survival, a gain of 4.2 points, 3.3 to 5.2 across the interval (the raw difference, 6.5 points, is confounded; the rest of the confounding is in internal_validity_adj). Survival in England is 9.5% at 30 days (2024), similar to Sweden's.

rows.label: Deaths averted per arrest a trainee is at
rows.explainer: The extra chance of CPR times what CPR adds to survival.

rows.label: Indirect deaths per direct death
rows.explainer: 0: the survival gain is all-cause survival after the arrest.

rows.label: Deaths averted per person trained (before adjustments)
RevivR: deaths averted before adjustments
The Circuit: cardiac arrests in the UK where ambulance services attempt resuscitation, per year

source.title: Resuscitation Council UK, 2025 Resuscitation Guidelines: Epidemiology of cardiac arrest
source.quote: NHS ambulance services attempt resuscitation in around 43,000 people each year in the UK.

rows.explainer: Every UK ambulance service uses The Circuit to tell 999 callers where the nearest registered defibrillator is, so the branch reaches every attempted resuscitation in the year (an ongoing service: one year's arrests against one year's cost, Convention 3).

rows.label: The Circuit: share of arrests where a bystander uses a public defibrillator (England, 2024)

source.title: Resuscitation Council UK, 2025 Resuscitation Guidelines: Epidemiology of cardiac arrest

rows.explainer: From the OHCAO registry, as the Resuscitation Council reports it (England, 2024); the network has grown to 118,800 devices registered, 18,500 new in the year (p. 32).

rows.label: The Circuit: share of bystander defibrillator uses that wouldn't happen without it
rows.explainer: Before The Circuit (2019) ambulance services kept their own, patchier lists; many defibrillators are used because they are on the wall where the arrest happens, without any dispatcher. No study measures the network's effect. Our judgment: a fifth of uses come from a caller sent to a device only the network knew of, 5% to 40%.

rows.label: The Circuit: survival gain per bystander defibrillator use (percentage points)
rows.explainer: Pollack et al. (Circulation 2018): in observed public arrests with a shockable rhythm, 66.5% of patients shocked by a bystander survived to discharge against 43.0% first shocked by the ambulance crew, 23.5 points. Only about half of arrests where a bystander brings a defibrillator have a shockable rhythm, and many uses the Circuit enables are at home, where survival is much lower than in public, so about 8 points per use, 4 to 15.

rows.label: The Circuit: deaths averted in the year (before adjustments)
Heart Helpline and peer support: dose against the education programmes in the trials
rows.explainer: The trials pooled by Anderson et al. (Cochrane 2017) gave education from one 40-minute session with a follow-up call to a four-week residential stay with 11 months of follow-up; most ran several sessions over months. A call with a cardiac nurse, or months in a peer community, is a fraction of that. Our judgment: a tenth of a trial programme's effect, 3% to 30% (the high end close to the trials' lightest programme). A brief nurse-led talk of about 20 minutes with a leaflet (the CABIN pilot, Caughers et al. 2026) is the nearest tested contact to a helpline call; it is feasible and improved knowledge in a pilot, with no outcome trial yet.

rows.label: Reading BHF's information: dose against the education programmes in the trials
rows.explainer: A reader spends minutes on a few pages or a booklet, against the trials' hours of taught and followed-up education. Reference class: in the ISLAND trial (Ivers et al., BMJ 2020, 2,632 patients after a heart attack), five tailored mail-outs over a year raised completion of cardiac rehabilitation from 27% to 32% but left medication adherence unchanged (odds ratio 0.98), a small fraction of what structured education does; a reader of a page or two gets less than five mail-outs. Our judgment: a hundredth of a trial programme's effect, 0.3% to 3%.

rows.label: Information and support: people reached, in trial programmes' worth of education
rows.explainer: Each channel's people times its dose, so the trials' effect per patient applies to the total.

rows.label: Yearly risk of death of people with coronary heart disease reached
rows.explainer: In the education trials 4.6% of the control groups died over follow-ups of six months to five years (Anderson et al. 2017); people with established heart disease in the UK, mostly over 65, die at a few percent a year. Our judgment: 3% a year, 2% to 5%.

rows.label: Fall in deaths with patient education (share of the risk)

source.title: Anderson et al. (2017), Patient education in the management of coronary heart disease, Cochrane Database Syst Rev CD008895 (abstract, Europe PMC)
source.quote: 189/5187 (3.6%) versus 222/4888 (4.6%); random effects risk ratio (RR) 0.80, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.05; moderate quality evidence

rows.explainer: 13 trials, 10,075 patients: a risk ratio of 0.80 for total mortality, so a 20% fall (the best guess), 95% CI from 40% fewer deaths to 5% more. The interval crosses no effect; the low end, 2%, is our judgment truncating the interval just above no effect (the engine's ranges are positive) rather than at a harm, since telephone support from nurses also lowers deaths (Inglis et al., Cochrane 2015: structured telephone support in heart failure, RR 0.87, 0.77 to 0.98) and education lowers readmissions (Ellis et al. 2025). The trials' weakness is in info_evidence_adj.

rows.label: Years over which the trials' effect is measured
rows.explainer: The trials' risk ratio is cumulative over their follow-up (at least six months, up to five years; Anderson et al. 2017): 4.6% of the control groups died, at about 3% a year roughly a year and a half, so the effect per trial programme is taken over 1.5 years, 1 to 3. A single call or page read fades sooner, but that is already in the dose rows, which scale a contact to a fraction of a trial programme; this row only says how long a trial programme's effect lasts.

rows.label: Information and support: deaths averted before adjustments
Information and support: gain in health-related quality of life per trial programme (0 to 1 scale)
rows.explainer: Education initiated in hospital raised quality of life by 0.28 standard deviations when delivered digitally (95% CI 0.07 to 0.48) and 1.19 in person (0.14 to 2.24) (Ellis et al., Eur J Prev Cardiol 2025, 32 trials); the Cochrane review found higher scores in some domains, not consistently (Anderson et al. 2017). Our judgment, not a sourced conversion: a health-utility score (EQ-5D, 0 to 1) varies between heart patients by about 0.2, so 0.28 SD would be about 0.05, the high end; the inconsistent Cochrane finding pulls the best guess to 0.02, low 0.005. Counted as a share of a year of healthy life, like a disability weight.

rows.label: Information and support: value of a death at 70 or older (units of value)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's five-year weights for 70–74 and 75–79 (their mean) and for 80 and over (85 and over has the same weight), mixed by the share of UK cardiovascular deaths at 70 or older that are at 80 or older.

rows.label: Information and support: value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: Deaths of heart patients at the ages UK cardiovascular deaths happen (GBD 2023, facts: death_ages: four in five at 70 or older), each at GiveWell's moral weight for its age (50–69 at the 50–74 band, 70 and over at the five-year weights; references: families/high-income-care.md), times the value-of-a-life slider.

rows.label: Share of deaths averted under age 5
rows.explainer: 0: cardiac arrests in young children are very rare, have other causes than in adults, and are rarely helped by adult CPR training or public defibrillators; the older ages are split below.

rows.label: Share of over-5 deaths averted at ages 5 to 14
rows.explainer: 0: arrests at school age are rare too (school defibrillators and CPR help some, as in Sam Mangoro's story in the annual report), far too few to move the age mix.

rows.label: Share of adult deaths averted at ages 15 to 49
rows.explainer: 55-65% of out-of-hospital cardiac arrests are in people aged 65 or over (Resuscitation Council UK); survivors are younger than all patients, because younger patients more often have shockable rhythms and witnessed arrests. Our judgment: 15% of survivors are under 50.

rows.label: Share of deaths averted at 50 and over that are at 75 and over
rows.explainer: Rich-country deaths are older than the 50 to 74 band, so the oldest survivors are valued at GiveWell's weight for ages 75 to 79 (a lower value, since fewer years remain) rather than the band's (references: families/high-income-care.md). About 30%, from the age mix of patients and survivors' younger skew. Cardiac-arrest survivors are younger than heart patients who die (GBD has no cause for cardiac arrest), so their oldest are valued at the 75–79 weight rather than mixed with 80 and over; the branch is under a fifth of this model's value.

rows.label: Illness averted, as a share of the deaths' value
rows.explainer: 0: the programme averts deaths, not illness; brain injury among some survivors, a harm, is in other_unmodelled_share instead (illness counted in one place only).

rows.label: Stillbirths averted per person
rows.explainer: 0: CPR training and defibrillators don't touch stillbirths.

rows.label: Later-life income gain per person, ln(consumption) per year
rows.explainer: 0: survivors are mostly past working age, and GiveWell's later-life income gain is for children's development, not adults saved.

rows.label: Years until the income gain starts
rows.explainer: Unused (no income gain); the skeleton's shared read is kept.

rows.label: Years the income gain lasts
Discounted ln(consumption) gain per person
Income shared with the household (GiveWell's multiplier)
Information and support: healthy years gained per trial programme's worth of education
rows.explainer: The quality-of-life gain for the years it lasts, per trial programme's worth (info_trial_equivalents); RevivR and The Circuit avert deaths only, so their illness is 0 (see morbidity_value_ratio).

rows.label: RevivR and The Circuit: internal validity of the registry studies
rows.explainer: Both survival gains come from registries, not trials (a trial of CPR against none would be unethical). Adjusting for witnessed arrests, location and rhythm removes much of the confounding, but arrests where bystanders act are still likelier to be survivable. 0.7, as GiveWell-style internal-validity adjustments for observational effects.

rows.label: RevivR and The Circuit: external validity
rows.explainer: Swedish and US registries in rich-country systems with similar ambulance times; app-trained bystanders may do less well than the trained bystanders in the studies.

rows.label: RevivR and The Circuit: trust in the evidence
Information and support: trust in the education trials
rows.explainer: The mortality effect is moderate-quality evidence whose interval crosses no effect, from a meta-analysis with possible small-study effects, and the quality-of-life gains are inconsistent (Anderson et al. 2017); the trials' programmes were structured and given to patients after an event, unlike readers who seek information themselves (the dose rows take the size of the contact; this takes the rest). Our judgment: 0.6, 0.35 to 0.9, a little below the 0.63 for the CPR registries because the effect itself is uncertain.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment
rows.formula: (revivr_deaths_unadj * cpr_evidence_adj + circuit_deaths_averted * cpr_evidence_adj + info_deaths_averted * info_evidence_adj) / (revivr_deaths_unadj + circuit_deaths_averted + info_deaths_averted)
rows.explainer: The deaths-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own (cpr_evidence_adj, info_evidence_adj).

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.explainer: The deaths-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own (revivr_, circuit_, info_counterfactual_adj).
rows.formula: (revivr_deaths_unadj * revivr_counterfactual_adj + circuit_deaths_averted * circuit_counterfactual_adj + info_deaths_averted * info_counterfactual_adj) / (revivr_deaths_unadj + circuit_deaths_averted + info_deaths_averted)

rows.label: RevivR: share of trainees who wouldn't have learned CPR elsewhere in those years
rows.explainer: Some RevivR users would have trained anyway, at work (first-aid courses), with St John Ambulance or the Red Cross, or at school (CPR is in England's secondary curriculum since 2020). extra_cpr_prob compares trained with untrained bystanders, so this takes out the trainees whose training would have come another way in the same years. 0.8, from most RevivR users being people with no other course, 0.6 to 0.95.

rows.label: The Circuit: share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: circuit_share_of_aed_uses already counts only the uses that wouldn't happen without the network (Convention 5).

rows.label: Information and support: share of readers and callers who wouldn't have found the same help elsewhere
rows.explainer: The trials' control groups had usual care (referral to a cardiologist or GP; Anderson et al. 2017), so what hospitals tell patients and cardiac rehabilitation are already netted out of the effect. What is left is help these readers and callers would have found elsewhere: the NHS website, other charities' pages and helplines, a GP's advice beyond usual care. BHF's information is the UK's main specialist source for heart patients and its nurse helpline has no NHS equivalent for most conditions. Our judgment: 55% wouldn't have come anyway, 30% to 80%.

rows.label: RevivR: BHF's share of the resources behind the training
rows.explainer: Trainees give 15 to 30 minutes each (190,000 people, about 60,000 hours, around £1m at UK median pay), teachers give lesson time, and Laerdal is BHF's partner on the app. BHF pays for the app, its promotion and the schools programme. Our judgment: BHF about 60% of the resources.

rows.label: RevivR: share of credit used
rows.explainer: BHF's share of the resources behind the training; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: The Circuit: BHF's share of the resources behind the defibrillator uses
rows.explainer: A use needs the device (118,800 registered, bought by communities, businesses and schools, about £1,000-1,500 each with pads and batteries over 8 to 10 years: of the order of £15-20m a year), its guardian's checks (80,000 volunteers), the 999 call handler and the network. BHF runs The Circuit with the Resuscitation Council UK, the ambulance chief executives and NHS England, and funds some devices. Our judgment: a tenth, 5% to 30%.

rows.label: The Circuit: share of credit used
rows.explainer: BHF's share of the resources behind the defibrillator uses; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Information and support: BHF's share of the resources
rows.explainer: BHF writes and pays for the information, the magazine and the nurses; Tesco part-funds the printed information and Royal Mail the accessible formats (p. 31), HealthUnlocked hosts the community and its members give each other their time. Our judgment: BHF 90%.

rows.label: Information and support: BHF's share of the credit
rows.explainer: BHF's share of the resources behind the information and support; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: This charity's share of the resources behind the outcome (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (revivr_deaths_unadj * revivr_attribution_share_shared + circuit_deaths_averted * circuit_attribution_share_shared + info_deaths_averted * info_attribution_share_shared) / (revivr_deaths_unadj + circuit_deaths_averted + info_deaths_averted)
rows.explainer: The deaths-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own share.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The deaths-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own share (revivr_, circuit_, info_attribution_share).

rows.label: RevivR: share of reported completions that are real, distinct UK trainees
rows.explainer: RevivR only: BHF's own app count, and some people complete it twice or outside the UK. The Circuit uses the registry's observed defibrillator use, and the information branch's reach is already a judgment with its doses, so neither takes this adjustment.

rows.label: Implementation (deaths-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.explainer: The deaths-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: RevivR applies revivr_implementation_adj; The Circuit (observed defibrillator use) and the information branch (reach already a judgment with its doses) take none, so 1.

rows.label: Others would have paid anyway (<1) or the money pulls others in (>1)
rows.explainer: 1: no government programme would fund a national CPR app, the defibrillator network or BHF's helpline in BHF's place soon (the Scottish Government's £2.5m for cardiac arrest survival in February 2026 funds devices and local response, which the network complements). Information the NHS already provides is in info_counterfactual_adj, and the devices others buy in attribution, so neither is counted again here.

rows.label: Years from a gift to its spending
rows.explainer: BHF spent £25.3m more than it raised this year, drawing down reserves (p. 64): a gift is spent at once.

rows.label: Years from spending to delivery
rows.explainer: The app and the network run continuously; training and dispatch follow the spending within the year.

rows.label: RevivR: years to the middle of a trainee's readiness
RevivR: discount for the wait until the benefits come
Wait until the benefits, discounted (deaths-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (revivr_deaths_unadj * revivr_wait_discount + circuit_deaths_averted * circuit_wait_discount + info_deaths_averted * info_wait_discount) / (revivr_deaths_unadj + circuit_deaths_averted + info_deaths_averted)
rows.explainer: The deaths-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own wait (revivr_, circuit_, info_wait_discount), each read at the shared discount rate.

rows.label: The Circuit: discount for the wait until the benefits come (the middle of the year)
Information and support: wait until the benefit, discounted
rows.explainer: The middle of the year or so the effect lasts, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: RevivR: missing-data step
rows.explainer: Thin: BHF counts the trainees, but no study measures what RevivR's training changes; how much more often a trainee gives CPR (extra_cpr_prob) and how long the training lasts are judgments, and the survival gain is from registries of bystander CPR in general. So the shared missing-data step applies (templates.md Convention 12).

rows.label: The Circuit: missing-data step
rows.explainer: Thin: the registry counts defibrillator uses, but the share that happen because the network sent someone (circuit_share_of_aed_uses) is our judgment and no study measures it. So the shared missing-data step applies (templates.md Convention 12).

rows.label: Information and support: missing-data step
rows.explainer: Thin: BHF reports contacts and page views but no outcomes; the readers, the doses and an effect from education trials delivered another way are judgments and research. So the shared missing-data step applies (templates.md Convention 12).

rows.label: Missing-data step (deaths-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (revivr_deaths_unadj * revivr_missing_data_adj + circuit_deaths_averted * circuit_missing_data_adj + info_deaths_averted * info_missing_data_adj) / (revivr_deaths_unadj + circuit_deaths_averted + info_deaths_averted)
rows.explainer: Every branch's outcome is thin (no measured outcome for BHF's own work), so each reads the shared slider; this average is for reading only.

rows.label: RevivR: all adjustments combined
rows.formula: cpr_evidence_adj * revivr_counterfactual_adj * revivr_attribution_share * revivr_implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * revivr_wait_discount * revivr_missing_data_adj

rows.label: The Circuit: all adjustments combined
rows.formula: cpr_evidence_adj * circuit_counterfactual_adj * circuit_attribution_share * leverage_funging_adj * circuit_wait_discount * circuit_missing_data_adj

rows.label: Information and support: product of adjustments
rows.formula: info_evidence_adj * info_counterfactual_adj * info_attribution_share * leverage_funging_adj * info_wait_discount * info_missing_data_adj

rows.label: All adjustments combined (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (revivr_deaths_unadj * revivr_total_adj + circuit_deaths_averted * circuit_total_adj + info_deaths_averted * info_total_adj) / (revivr_deaths_unadj + circuit_deaths_averted + info_deaths_averted)
rows.explainer: Each branch's own product of adjustments, weighted by its deaths averted before adjustment (for reading; each branch's outcome applies its own).

rows.label: Treatment costs averted, as a share of value
rows.explainer: 0: GiveWell's 20% is for illness averted in poor countries; a cardiac-arrest survivor in the UK adds NHS treatment costs rather than saving them (paid by the NHS, not counted as a harm here).

rows.label: Rebound effects, as a share of value
rows.explainer: 0: there is no immunity or similar rebound for cardiac arrest.

rows.label: Investment of income gains, as a share of value
rows.explainer: 0: the model counts no income gain.

rows.label: Other benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of value
rows.explainer: Harm: some cardiac-arrest survivors live with brain injury (most survivors to discharge have good neurological outcomes, a minority don't), so a death averted is worth a little less than a full life. Benefits not counted: trained people also help in choking and other emergencies; awareness campaigns and information that prompt earlier diagnosis (a reader who asked for a scan that found a blocked artery, p. 30) or a quicker call to 999; reassurance for families, and carers who read the information and help the patient act on it. Net about zero, -10% to +15%.
